newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajikistan hopeful about negotiations on hostages.
newsitem.headline: Tajikistan hopeful about negotiations on hostages.

text.p: Tajikistan said on Friday negotiations with rebels holding up to 16 U.N. officials, Red Cross workers and journalists were looking hopeful.
Four employees of the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR were kidnapped on Thursday by the rebels, who are believed to have seized up to 12 other hostages in the former Soviet republic.
"The negotiations are hopeful," Zafar Saidov, spokesman for Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov, told Reuters in the capital Dushanbe.
But he added: "No one has been released."
The hostage-takers are part of a group commanded by Rizvon Sadirov, who used to fight for the Islamic opposition but whose loyalties are now unclear.
They are demanding free passage for other group members to return from neighbouring Afghanistan.
Saidov said the head of the presidential guard, Gafar Mirzoyev, was on his way to negotiate with the rebels.
Officials say they expect the rebels to hand over four Russian journalists, taken hostage earlier this week, to Mirzoyev's negotiating team on Friday.
On Thursday, Russian officials threatened to use force to free the hostages.
However, Saidov said force was not being considered. "By no means will military force be used," he said.

The UNHCR said on Thursday it had had no contact with its four representatives -- an expatriate from Nigeria, a Tajik security guard and two Tajik drivers -- since they went missing in the centre of the capital with two marked U.N. cars.

U.N. military observers in Tajikistan said the four were captured by the same rebel group that seized four U.N. military observers from Austria, Switzerland and Ukraine, two Red Cross workers and four Russian journalists.
UNHCR figures on the hostages differed slightly, putting the number of kidnapped military observers at five and the number of journalists who had been seized at five.

Tajikistan, a mountainous country bordering China, has been racked by a bitter four-year civil war but a ceasefire agreed between the government and the armed Islamic opposition last December appears to be holding.
